catalog_quote: In a phrase, which of course may consist of a single word, only the last word is accented. Accent is thus a property of phrases rather than of words, but word boundaries and the internal phonological structure of words determine in the following manner the syllabic element on which the accent falls. In the last word of the phrase, accent is placed by this rule common to many Malay dialects: if the penultimate syllable contains schwa, accent the syllabic elemenr on the last syllable; otherwise accent the syllabic element of the penult. Impressionistically, this accent seems to consist primarily of a rise in pitch, often accompanied by an increase in duration and intensity. (Wallace 1976)
sweep_summary: Betawi (beta1252) is in the catalog as PHRASAL on a carried Wallace 1976: 56-59 quote. The only title-works with stress in the title, Roosman 2006 (LOT 129), was already held by the project and was read in full: it summarises Wallace (pp. 29-30: accent on the penult of the phrase-final word, final if the penult has schwa or the word is prefix + monosyllabic stem, monosyllables always accented) and reports her own production/perception experiments (p. 59, p. 66, pp. 135-136, 161-162), concluding that BM has phrasal accent only and no word stress; the perception numbers (100% penult baseline, 50% shift to ultima with schwa penult, 50% shift sentence-finally) refine the categorical rule. Two further sources were pursued: Muhadjir 1981 (NUSA 11, the English edition of Muhadjir 1977, which Roosman cites for 'no word stress') was downloaded from sealang and scanned (pp. 1-44); its only statement is p. 15, 'there are no suprasegmental phonemes in this dialect', consistent with the classification. Van Heuven, Roosman & van Zanten 2008 (Lingua 118: 1271-1287, DOI 10.1016/j.lingua.2007.09.005) is paywalled with no open copy found; Wallace 1976 remains ProQuest-only (archive.org and HathiTrust have no record). Recommendation: keep PHRASAL; make Roosman 2006: 66 the eyes-on deciding statement (Wallace 1976 stays as the carried placement rule); note the Glottolog URL for Roosman 2006 is dead and the working one ishttps://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/129_fulltext.pdf.org/HathiTrust probes was not possible. Records: and.

new_statements.quote: I. Accent falls on the penultimate syllable (100%). II. If the penultimate syllable contains a schwa, accent shifts in 50% to the ultimate syllable (50% penultimate, 50% ultimate). III. If the target is in sentence-final position, accent shifts in 50% to the ultimate syllable (50% penultimate, 50% ultimate). [...] However, accent shifts because of the position of the target in the sentence. This shift of perceived accent shows that BM has phrasal accent only; it has no word stress with which the phrasal accent can be aligned.

new_statements.locator: p. 66 (ch. III §3.5.2.2, auditory perception results for Betawi Malay; PDF page 78)
new_statements.reading: First-hand experimental statement: Betawi Malay has no word stress; prominence is a phrase-level accent realised by pitch movement on focused words only, heard on the penult by default, with a 50% shift to the ultima when the penult has schwa and a 50% shift to the ultima sentence-finally (100% ultima expected when both hold). This confirms the catalog's PHRASAL coding and the penult-unless-schwa placement carried from Wallace 1976, and refines it: the schwa-driven shift and the boundary-driven shift are gradient in perception, not categorical, and no pitch accent appears on unfocused words.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'phrasal' (accent on last word of phrase; penult unless schwa, then final; no word stress) rests on Wallace 1976 quoted second-hand (evidence: quoted second-hand from StressTyp2, the original not read) but is independently and directly supported by instrumental work we hold: Roosman 2007 ch. 5 p. 100 (held, verified at page) and now Roosman 2006 LOT diss. p. 66, 78-79, 163 (downloaded, open access), which conclude BM 'has phrasal accent only; it has no word stress'. Roosman refines Wallace: accent lands on penult or final within a two-syllable window, with sentence-final position (not only penult schwa) pulling it to the ultima; Wallace's schwa->final rule holds only sentence-finally. That refinement could be added to the primary-stress rule but does not change classification phrasal, domain=phrase, edge=right. StressTyp2's weight-sensitive P/P word-stress coding is the outlier, already flagged in 'contra'. Suggest upgrading the strength of the evidence from carried-q

sources.quote: p. 26: 'Betawi Malay, on the other hand, is a language that, like Indonesian, does not have word stress (Muhadjir, 1977) but it does have phrasal accent (Wallace, 1976).' p. 29: 'Wallace notices that the domain of the accent is the phrase rather than the word. His impression is that there is no word stress in BM.' p. 30: 'According to Wallace (1976:56-59), the accent is usually on the penultimate syllable of the last word in a phrase in BM. [...] The accent goes to the final position if the penultimate has schwa (a), or if the last word of the phrase is made up of a monosyllabic stem preceded by a prefix (b). A monosyllabic word is always accented (c).' p. 66: 'This shift of perceived accent shows that BM has phrasal accent only; it has no word stress with which the phrasal accent can be aligned.'

Own results, p. 66: in a perception test on focused disyllables, accent was heard on the penult 100% of the time in the baseline case; with a schwa penult it shifted to the ultima in 50% of judgements; sentence-finally it shifted to the ultima in 50%; with both conditions it should be 100% ultima.
